analysis.one_liner: Opens federal oil shale, offshore waters, and the Alaska refuge to oil and gas drilling, and fast-tracks Keystone XL.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 237-187 on a mostly party-line vote in February 2012, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill started as an oil shale bill and grew into a package of energy provisions. It would have locked in Bush-era oil shale regulations against any court challenge, forced lease sales on federal oil shale, offshore waters, and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, stripped the president's authority over the Keystone XL pipeline permit, and let the Interior Secretary cut royalties to spur oil shale development. It also included faster permitting for wind, solar, and geothermal projects and a trust fund to restore the Gulf Coast after the Deepwater Horizon spill.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain mandated access to federal oil shale in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming, to offshore areas in the Gulf, off Virginia, and off Southern California, and to the Arctic refuge's coastal plain — with the Interior Secretary authorized to cut royalties and fees to encourage oil shale development. The Keystone XL pipeline would get a federal permit within 30 days, with the president's permit authority removed, and the operator could start building outside Nebraska while the Nebraska route was still under review. Wind, solar, and geothermal developers would get faster environmental review on federal lands, and Gulf Coast states would get a trust fund to restore the region after the Deepwater Horizon spill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies; Keystone pipeline developer

how_it_helps.text: Declares the 2008 Bureau of Land Management oil shale regulations and planning decisions to satisfy 'all legal and procedural requirements under any law' — including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act — and orders the Interior Secretary to implement the oil shale leasing program with no further action, making the rules effectively lawsuit-proof.

Requires a lease sale of 10 more research-and-development oil shale parcels within 180 days and at least five commercial oil shale lease sales of at least 25,000 acres each by January 1, 2016, and authorizes the Secretary to temporarily reduce royalties, fees, and bonus payments to encourage oil shale production.

Removes the president's authority over the Keystone XL pipeline: it declares no presidential permit is required, orders the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to issue a permit within 30 days (deemed issued if it does nothing), treats the State Department's 2011 environmental review as final, and lets construction proceed outside Nebraska while a route change in Nebraska is reviewed.

Mandates offshore oil and gas lease sales in the central Gulf of Mexico, off Virginia, and in the Southern California planning area, requires at least half the unleased acreage in the most resource-rich offshore planning areas to be offered for leasing, repeals offshore leasing moratoria near Florida, and opens the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to a competitive leasing program.

Carries provisions with broader benefit: it shares new offshore leasing revenue with coastal states, creates a Gulf Coast Restoration Trust Fund for the five Gulf states hit by the Deepwater Horizon spill, streamlines environmental review for wind, solar, and geothermal projects on federal lands, and exempts small geothermal test wells from full environmental impact statements.
Directs the Secretary to encourage use of U.S. workers and U.S.-made equipment in construction under the bill, reflecting stated intent to support American manufacturing jobs.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the public would bear the costs: federal land and waters would be opened with the Interior Secretary allowed to cut royalties and fees for oil shale, reducing what taxpayers collect; the bill's deeming clauses would shut courts and affected communities out of challenging oil shale, offshore, and Arctic refuge decisions; environmental review would be narrowed so agencies need not consider any alternative besides leasing; and coastal towns would take on the risk of new offshore drilling — the bill itself orders a study of potential harm to Florida Gulf coast fishing and tourism industries. The Arctic refuge's coastal plain, closed to development since 1980, would be opened to leasing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, coastal communities, and the Arctic refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill declares its 2008 oil shale regulations, the Keystone environmental review, and various offshore reviews to satisfy 'all legal and procedural requirements under any law,' including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Endangered Species Act — meaning citizens, local communities, and conservation groups could not sue to challenge those decisions, and agencies would not have to analyze any alternative to leasing.

It authorizes the Interior Secretary to temporarily reduce royalties, fees, rentals, and bonus payments for oil shale leases to encourage development, meaning the federal treasury — and by extension taxpayers — could collect less for resources owned by the public.

It opens the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas leasing and mandates offshore sales in areas long off-limits, including the Southern California planning area (where state consistency requirements would be declared inapplicable) and waters within 125 miles of Florida's coast; the bill itself requires an economic impact survey of harm to Florida's fishing and tourism industries.

The Keystone provision would strip the president of permit authority over a cross-border pipeline and deem a permit granted if regulators miss a 30-day deadline, removing review in exchange for construction jobs that are temporary and fuel that is projected largely for export.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles together provisions of very different value. The Gulf Coast restoration fund and streamlined permitting for genuinely renewable projects are real benefits, and supporters made a fair argument that more domestic energy production supports jobs. But the bill's center of gravity is a large transfer of publicly owned resources — oil shale, offshore tracts, and the Arctic refuge — to private energy companies, financed partly by royalty cuts and achieved by legally barring citizens and courts from challenging the underlying environmental decisions. An honest reading is that the jobs rhetoric was broad while the enforceable commitments to workers ('encourage' U.S. workers and equipment, 'when possible and practicable') were nonbinding.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House on a mostly party-line vote, but the Senate never voted on it, and on the final day of the Congress the House routinely laid it on the table, ending it.

narrative.text: Representative Doug Lamborn introduced the bill in November 2011 as a single-purpose oil shale measure with zero cosponsors, and it was referred to the Natural Resources Committee.
The committee expanded it into a much larger energy package and reported it amended on February 9, 2012, by a 27-16 vote.

The reported version added a Keystone XL title that would remove the president's permit authority and force a permit within 30 days, plus offshore leasing, Arctic refuge leasing, coastal state revenue sharing, and the Gulf Coast RESTORE Act.

The House considered it in February 2012 under a rule giving one hour of debate; Democrats offered amendments on subjects like environmental review and drilling restrictions, and most were rejected on voice and recorded votes.

Representative Kathy Castor's motion to send the bill back with instructions to block new drilling near the Great Lakes and the Everglades failed 176-241, with 174 of 192 Democrats in favor and only 9 opposed; just 2 of 242 Republicans supported it.
The bill passed the House 237-187, with 216 of 242 Republicans voting yes and only 21 of 192 Democrats — a near-total party split.
The Senate never took up the bill. On January 3, 2013, the last day of the 112th Congress, the House laid it on the table — a routine step that ended any further action.
One piece of the bill did survive by another route: the RESTORE Act's Gulf Coast restoration trust fund was enacted separately in mid-2012 as part of the highway bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing in the bill became law, so oil and gas companies did not gain the mandated lease access, the Keystone operator did not get its automatic permit, and the president's authority over the pipeline and existing protections for the Arctic refuge and offshore areas remained in place. Gulf Coast states ultimately won the restoration fund anyway through separate legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public protections stayed; energy industry gained nothing

for.name: Doug Lamborn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the oil shale bill in November 2011 with no cosponsors.

for.name: Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: His committee grew the oil shale bill into a package adding Keystone XL, offshore leasing, and Arctic refuge titles, and reported it amended by a 27-16 vote.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.role: Committee controlling floor procedure (Chair David Dreier, R-CA)
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 547) giving the bill one hour of debate and waiving all points of order against its consideration.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the House-passed bill to a Senate vote; it died without Senate action.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Had denied the Keystone XL permit weeks before the House vote and opposed legislation stripping his permit authority; the bill never reached his desk.

against.name: 174 of 192 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted for the motion to recommit to block new drilling near the Great Lakes and the Everglades, and 166 of 192 voted no on final passage.

against.name: House Democratic amendment sponsors (Markey, Eshoo, Rush, Doyle, Polis, Capps, Deutch, Thompson)
against.role: Ranking members and Natural Resources Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Offered a series of amendments during floor debate; nearly all were rejected.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 216 of 242 Republicans voted yes while only 21 of 192 Democrats did, and the earlier motion to recommit went the opposite way (Democrats 174-9, Republicans 2-232).

industries.note: The bill would have mandated lease sales on federal oil shale, offshore tracts in the Gulf, off Virginia, and off Southern California, and opened the Arctic refuge's coastal plain — while authorizing royalty cuts and barring most legal challenge. Federal resources would flow to private producers on terms the public could not contest.

The bill would have removed the presidential permit requirement and forced a federal permit within 30 days, with approval deemed automatic if regulators missed the deadline — a direct shortcut around the review process then underway.

The bill would have let project applicants limit environmental review to two alternatives and shortened comment windows, and exempted small geothermal test wells from environmental impact statements — faster, cheaper permitting on federal lands.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast restoration and coastal economies
industries.note: The RESTORE Act title would have deposited Clean Water Act penalties from the Deepwater Horizon spill into a trust fund for restoring the ecosystems and economies of the five Gulf states; this provision passed later as a standalone law.

industries.industry: Florida Gulf coast fishing and tourism
industries.note: The bill would have repealed leasing moratoria in parts of the eastern Gulf within 125 miles of Florida while ordering a survey of adverse effects on Florida fishing and tourism — new drilling risk alongside some zoning and military-use protections.
